paragraphs.text: This leaf comes from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is), in the north of Mengla County in Xishuangbanna, on the east side of the Lancang River, the upper Mekong. The area is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and its town has long been where leaf from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed.

The leaf was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition), a method developed to bring about in weeks the change that raw pu’er reaches only after years of keeping. In [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) the sun-dried leaf is wetted and heaped, and the microbes in the heap make their own heat. The pile is covered to hold that warmth in, turned about once a week to spread it and let in air, and kept below about 65°C so the leaf does not char. Once dried, this leaf was pressed into a cake.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
